pageDesc: User manual for desktop and mobile

about.title: What is 大懒猫写作
about.body:
BigLazyCat Writer is a local-first writing app with AI built in, for desktop (Windows / macOS / Linux) and mobile (Android / iOS). Long-form drafting, bidirectional links, mind maps, canvases, research material, typeset books and WeChat publishing all live in one app.

## Your data stays on your devices

Everything is ordinary files: a piece is a Markdown file, a work is a folder, mind maps are `.xmind`, canvases are `.canvas`. Open them with any editor, back them up with any cloud drive or Git, and take them along when you switch computers. Your work is never locked inside a cloud database.

## Desktop

The full workstation: a WYSIWYG editor, the AI workbench and agent, PDF reading and annotation, OCR, global search, mind maps, flow canvases and presentations, and a plugin center. Multi-tab, split view and multi-window layouts are supported, and a built-in MCP Server lets external AI clients drive the app.

Typeset books and WeChat publishing ship as official plugins — install them from the plugin center first, see [Official Plugins](#/plugins/official).

## Mobile

Shares the same file formats and sync protocol as the desktop. Capture ideas, edit chapters, mind maps and canvases on the go, with selection AI, summary, proofreading and sharing on board.

## Licensing

The desktop edition is a one-time purchase, yours forever. Every download starts a fully featured 30-day trial without an activation code; after the trial the app turns read-only — your work stays untouched, and activation restores everything. The mobile app and the portal's online tools are free.

## Next steps

- First time here: start with [Download & Install](#/quickstart/download);
- To configure AI: see [AI Model Setup](#/quickstart/aiSetup);
- New to Markdown: read [Markdown Basics](#/syntax/markdownBasics) first.

changelog.title: Changelog
changelog.body:
This page lists what each release changes. Updates never touch your work: content lives in local files and stays intact afterwards.

## How to update

1. The app checks once at startup, then every 24 hours. A new version only raises a notice in the top bar — nothing installs by itself;
2. Click that notice, or open "Settings → About", to check, download, skip a version, or save and restart to finish;
3. Packages are verified by SHA-256 and signature, and the app falls back to Gitee when GitHub is unreachable. You can also download the installer from the [portal home](/#download) and install over the current version.

## Check your version

Open "Settings → About" in the desktop app.

download.title: Download & Install (Desktop)
download.body:
The desktop app runs on Windows, macOS and Linux; installers are on the portal home page.

## Download

Open the [portal home](/#download), pick your system in the download section (Windows / macOS / Linux); every installer is offered from both GitHub and Gitee.

## Install

1. Run the installer and follow the prompts (a portable build is also available);
2. Start BigLazyCat Writer — the first launch initializes local data, which takes a moment;
3. No activation code needed: every install starts a 30-day full-feature trial.

## Where your work lives

Everything you write goes into the local creation area (an ordinary folder) by default. To move computers, copy that folder; a portable mode for USB drives is supported too.

account.title: Account & Activation

firstWork.title: Create Your First Work
firstWork.body:
A walk through the basics — creating a novel and letting AI push it forward.

## Create a work

Open "All documents" in the desktop app and click + in the catalog. A single piece is created directly; for a series, create a folder first, then files inside it.

## Write the first chapter

The body is Markdown with WYSIWYG editing; tables, code highlighting, formulas and images work out of the box. When you need references, switch to the two-column mode and put the built-in browser or the materials library on the right.

## Let AI push it forward

Select a paragraph or give instructions in the outline: generate an outline, continue writing, polish, or come up with titles. AI uses the models you configured under "Settings → AI services" — see [AI Model Setup](#/quickstart/aiSetup).

## Build connections

Type `[[` while writing to link chapters with setting notes and ideas — see [Bidirectional Links](#/writing/bilink). Tag chapters to find them later with [Global Search](#/writing/search).

## Save and roll back

The body saves automatically. Every chapter keeps version snapshots; if a rewrite goes wrong, recover it from [Version History](#/writing/versionHistory).

tour.title: A Tour of the Desktop
tour.body:
The main window has three parts: navigation and creation folders on the left, a tabbed workspace in the middle, and a top bar for sync, focus and window controls.

## The sidebar

From top to bottom:

- **Trends**: your daily dashboard — total items, total words, words written today and today's AI tokens, followed by the writing trend, a year-long heatmap, recently opened items and topic distribution. Pomodoro focus stats live here too;
- **All documents**: the main writing page — work catalog, body editor and the AI panel — see [Editor & Writing](#/writing/editor);
- **Assets**: image library and AI image generation — see [AI Image Generation](#/ai/imageGen);
- **Web**: built-in browser and web clipping — see [Browser & Web Clipping](#/materials/browser);
- **Plugin Center**: install, enable and manage plugins — see [Official Plugins](#/plugins/official).

A star entry, **Favorites**, sits under "All documents" and gathers everything you have starred.

Below the main menu are two pages: **Tags** (see [Tag System](#/writing/tags)) and **Links**, which holds the bidirectional-link graph (see [Relationship Graph](#/writing/graph)).

Underneath is **Local creation area**: the folders you have added. Click one to open its contents; right-click to create, rename or delete.

The bottom of the sidebar always holds Settings, the theme picker and the light/dark switch. Settings has 17 sections — see [Settings Overview](#/quickstart/settings).

## The top bar

On the left: brand mark, menu toggle, catalog toggle (only on "All documents") and the update entry. On the right: sync status, multi-tab toggle, side-by-side workspace toggle, Pomodoro timer, AI panel toggle and window controls.

The close button hides the window to the system tray; quitting goes through the tray menu.

## The workspace

The middle area is tabbed: different items get their own tab, the same item jumps to its existing tab, and a tab can be moved into a standalone window. In split view each side has its own tabs, with a draggable divider between them.

The AI panel sits on the right of the writing area, and the dot under the text only reports save status.

settings.title: Settings Overview

aiSetup.title: AI Model Setup
aiSetup.body:
AI features run on models you configure yourself: built-in providers GLM, DeepSeek, Gemini and OpenAI, plus any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

## Desktop

1. Open "Settings → AI services";
2. Pick a provider or choose custom, then fill in the endpoint and model name;
3. Enter the API key and save;
4. Confirm with "Test connection".

## Mobile

1. Open "Settings → AI models";
2. Enter an OpenAI-compatible endpoint and API key, then tap "Fetch model list" and pick a model.

API keys are stored only in the system keychain / keystore.

## Network proxy

If you cannot reach the provider, set a proxy for AI requests (http / https / socks5) under "Settings → Network proxy". It applies to model requests only — sync and the built-in browser are unaffected.

## Portal online tools

For the online tools (canvas, mind maps, PDF reading), fill in the "Model configuration" panel at the top; the configuration stays in your browser only.

## Cost and privacy

Model requests go directly to your provider — the platform never touches them or adds a markup. API keys stay on your machine; usage and billing are settled in your provider account.

editor.title: The Editor

vim.title: Vim Editing Mode
vim.body:
Writers with Vim habits can enable Vim-style editing in the desktop editor: the keys and feel follow Vim, while rendering stays WYSIWYG.

## Enter and exit

Click "Enter Vim-style editing" in the editor toolbar; click again to exit. A persistent status strip shows the current mode, line number and key hints; `Esc` always returns to NORMAL.

## Three modes

| Mode | Enter by | For |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NORMAL | default; `Esc` returns | movement and line ops; the caret sits between characters |
| INSERT | `i` / `a` | writing; `Esc` returns to NORMAL |
| VISUAL | `v` (characterwise) / `V` (linewise) | select, then yank or delete |

## Motion

- `h` `j` `k` `l`: left, down, up, right (arrow keys work too); column position survives line wraps;
- `w` / `b`: word forward / backward; `0` line start, `$` line end (`Home` / `End` same);
- `gg` to the top, `G` to the bottom; a number plus `G` jumps to that line, e.g. `12G`.

## Editing

- `i` writes before the caret, `a` after; `o` / `O` open a line below / above and start writing;
- `x` deletes the character under the caret; `u` undoes the last change;
- Line ops: `yy` yanks the line, `dd` deletes it, `p` pastes; deleted text lands in the clipboard too, recoverable with `p`;
- In tables, `Tab` / `Shift+Tab` move between cells.

## Selection

`v` selects characterwise, `V` linewise; with a selection, `y` yanks and `d` deletes, `Esc` cancels. Yank and paste use the system clipboard, sharing it with ordinary copy.

## Caveats

- Vim mode is desktop-only; a few structures like multi-line cells report "not supported" and leave the body untouched;
- Keystrokes from IME composition are never intercepted — typing Chinese works normally;
- Keys that match no command only show a hint and do nothing — safe to experiment.

bilink.title: Bidirectional Links
bilink.body:
Bidirectional links connect two documents: link B from A, and A automatically appears in B's backlinks. Character sheets, foreshadowing and research all chain together with them.

## Insert a link

Desktop:

1. Place the caret in the body and type `[[` — a file list pops up;
2. Pick the target document and press Enter, or click the "Bidirectional link" toolbar button;
3. Click the created link to jump to the target.

Mobile:

1. Place the caret in the body and type `[[`, or tap "Insert bidirectional link" in the bottom toolbar;
2. Search and pick the target, then confirm.

Links can carry an alias: `[[document|display text]]` — only the alias shows in the body.

## Backlinks

Open a document on the desktop and the backlink panel lists everything linking to it; click a source to jump there. On mobile, the "Backlinks" toolbar button shows the same list.

Halfway through a chapter and need a character detail? Follow the backlink to the character sheet and jump straight back.

## Typical uses

- One document per character; `[[` to it whenever they appear;
- Link foreshadowing chapters to a tracking list, then sweep the backlinks when it's time to pay off;
- Cross-reference clippings, idea notes and chapters, then organize with [Tags](#/writing/tags).

For the whole network at a glance — and for finding unconnected documents — see [Relationship Graph](#/writing/graph).

tags.title: Tags
tags.body:
Tags tie all content together by topic: tag chapters, images and prompts with the same tag, then find them all in one click.

## Applying tags

- While writing, tag suggestions pop up inline — type and pick;
- Images and prompts take tags in their own pages.

## Managing tags

The "Tags" page in the left navigation manages the tags themselves; the whole bidirectional-link network lives on the "Links" page (see [Relationship Graph](#/writing/graph)). The Tags page offers tree and list layouts, pinning for favorites, and this month's new-tag counts. Bulk operations for periodic cleanup:

- **Merge tags**: fold "主角" and "男主" into one;
- **Unify colors**: one color per tag family;
- **Batch delete** and **purge unused**: drop tags nobody references anymore.

## Finding content by tag

Click any tag to list every linked work, chapter, canvas, image and prompt; click a result to jump there. When a tag search falls short, supplement with [Global Search](#/writing/search).

articleProperties.title: Article Properties & Frontmatter
articleProperties.body:
Each document's YAML frontmatter is its property card: status, summary, tags and custom properties live there, powering property filters and dynamic views. The "Properties" button at the top of the editor opens the panel; changes save themselves.

## The panel

- Read-only system info with a lock icon — title, id, revision — plus the three fixed properties: status, summary, tags;
- Changes save about half a second after typing stops, with the save status on top; closing the panel, switching documents and quitting the app all wait for the save;
- Failed saves keep your edits — click "Retry save"; on a concurrent-edit conflict you get a prompt, and unsaved edits are never lost.

## Fixed properties

- **Status**: draft / serializing / finished — pick one;
- **Summary**: a blurb quoted directly by cards and lists;
- **Tags**: Enter or comma turns input into tag chips; the × removes one. `#tags` found in the body plus AI-applied tags are listed separately under "recognized tags", each clickable back to its spot.

## Custom properties

"Add property": name it, pick a type, set a value, confirm with the checkmark. A property's type icon opens rename / retype / delete.

- Four types: text, number, date, boolean; property names accept Chinese;
- Unconfirmed rows never reach the file;
- Names colliding with system fields (`id`, `revision`, `tags`…) are refused at save.

## What is frontmatter?

Properties are written straight into the document's YAML frontmatter — the block between two `---` lines at the top of the file. Open the `.md` in any editor and it's there, hand-editable as long as it stays valid YAML. Broken YAML blocks property writes; fix it first, then use the panel again. The body and annotations live outside the frontmatter and are unaffected.

## Searching by property

`Ctrl+Shift+T` global search takes property conditions; multiple conditions default to AND:

| Condition | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `tag:人物` | the tag and its children |
| `status:draft` | drafts |
| `prop.project:雾城` | custom property equals a value |
| `prop.project:"雾 城"` | quote values containing spaces |
| `words:>=3000` | at least 3000 words |
| `updated:<-30d` | modified more than 30 days ago |
| `has:prop.source` | the property exists |

Comparisons ` = != > >= < <=` are supported; dates accept `YYYY-MM-DD`, `today`, `this-week` and relative days. Plain keywords also hit property values. A property hit opens the properties panel; a body hit keeps locating in the text — see [Global Search](#/writing/search).

## Dynamic views

The funnel icon at the top of "All documents" opens the view dialog: add filter rows (AND / OR) and combine keywords with folder scopes. Name it and click "Create" to save a dynamic view — results recompute as properties and files change. Views are stored locally; cross-device sync is not available yet.

graph.title: Relationship Graph

search.title: Global Search
search.body:
Global search sweeps the entire creation area at once: article bodies, PDFs, images, mind maps, presentations and canvases. The desktop default shortcut is `Ctrl+Shift+T`, remappable in settings.

## Use

1. Press `Ctrl+Shift+T` to summon the search window;
2. Type keywords — spaces separate terms, results rank by relevance;
3. Click a result to jump to the source, with the hit highlighted.

## The index

Search runs on a local index. the search index under "Settings → General" shows index statistics; with very large libraries or incomplete results, rebuild the index once.

On mobile, the search box at the top of the creation area searches local content.

flowMode.title: Focus Writing (Fullscreen & Flow Mode)
flowMode.body:
Two focus switches on the desktop: fullscreen writing hides every piece of interface, and flow mode fades in sentence by sentence, showing only the text near your caret.

## Fullscreen writing (F11)

Press `F11` — only the body remains. `Esc` or another `F11` exits.

## Flow mode (Ctrl+I)

Press `Ctrl+I`. Sentences fade in one by one and interface noise drops to a minimum; pair it with the pomodoro timer (phases and rounds adjustable). Pick the focus granularity in the editor settings drawer: current line / paragraph / content block; colors follow the theme or fix to light / dark.

Both modes require a single-pane editor; `Esc` exits either one.

multiwindow.title: Multi-Window & Split View
multiwindow.body:
When one screen isn't enough, the desktop offers three ways to widen the workspace.

## Side-by-side workspaces (split view)

Click "Side-by-side workspaces" in the top bar — the window splits into two panes, each with its own tabs. Drag the divider to set the ratio (20%–80%); double-click restores 50/50; a pane collapses automatically once all its tabs close. Writing on the left with a PDF open on the right is the classic combination.

## Standalone windows

Right-click a tab and choose "Open in standalone window" — the tab moves to a new window you can drag to another screen. Close the window and the tab returns to its original spot in the main window. The built-in browser opens in the main window only.

## Tab management

Drag to reorder tabs within a pane; right-click a tab to close others, close to the right, or close everything.

versionHistory.title: Version History
versionHistory.body:
Every chapter keeps version snapshots. Deleted by accident, mangled by a rewrite, killed by a crash — recoverable.

## Where snapshots come from

The body autosaves, and each save records a version snapshot; after an abnormal exit, reopening the app restores the latest draft state.

## Browse and restore

Open the editor's "Version history" panel:

- A timeline lists every snapshot; click to preview;
- One click restores a selected version as the current content;
- Snapshots you don't need can be deleted.

## A habit worth keeping

Save manually before a major rewrite to leave a "before the surgery" anchor; before handing a manuscript to anyone, glance at the diff against the previous version.

appearance.title: Appearance & Themes
appearance.body:
A theme decides how the whole app looks: interface, editor body and WeChat export share one theme — switch it and everything follows.

## Built-in themes

"Settings → Themes" offers 10 built-ins — pick one and it applies:

| Theme | Style |
| --- | --- |
| Default | cool frosted glass, amber headings, light and airy |
| GitHub style | system sans-serif, blue links — the familiar technical-doc look |
| Festival | warm rice-paper background, vermilion chapter seals, Song typeface; WeChat export adds covers, section heads and a TOC |
| Blue tech | restrained tech blue, centered serif headings, dark code windows |
| Academic | LaTeX-like: serif body, graded headings, three-line tables |
| Green rest | warm off-white paper with soft green accents — low-strain long reading |
| Lavender | soft purple headings and quote cards, light and translucent |
| Mint cards | hard-shadow white cards with highlighter marks — for reviews and comparisons |
| Breeze magazine | forest green and warm paper, magazine layout |
| Newspaper | newspaper masthead and double rules; chapter headings in black-on-white |

## Custom themes

A theme is just a folder: the core is `theme.css` (body styles), with optional `ui.css` (interface colors). No CSS skills required:

- **Have AI make one**: click "Customize with AI" in settings and hand the generated prompt to an external AI (with MCP services on); the AI writes the theme and installs it automatically;
- **Import one**: "Import theme" takes a .css file; or drop theme files straight into the folder under "Open theme folder" — the app watches the directory and loads changes automatically;
- **Edit by hand**: the panel embeds a CSS editor; `Ctrl+S` applies instantly;
- Theme metadata lives in a header comment: `@name`, `@description`, `@accent` and friends; colors after a `/* @dark */` comment apply to dark mode;
- Broke a built-in theme? "Restore built-in themes" returns it to factory condition.

Themes downloaded from anywhere work by dropping them in; deleting the current theme falls back to the default.

## Light and dark

"Settings → General → Appearance": light / dark / follow system. Every theme ships both a light and a dark face; this switch only picks which one is live. A theme without dark-specific colors keeps its light paper in dark mode — never force-inverted. The sun/moon button in the top bar is the same switch.

## Wallpaper

"Settings → General → Wallpaper" puts an image behind the editor desktop:

- Import a local image (PNG / JPEG / WebP, up to 20 MB), or pick "Default grid" for the theme's own backdrop only;
- Tune interface opacity separately for 7 regions: editor, menu bar, tabs, top status bar, toolbar, volume/chapter panel and AI panel — lower values show more wallpaper;
- Dark mode dims the wallpaper automatically to spare your eyes.

## Shortcuts

Every app-level shortcut is remappable under "Settings → Shortcuts": quick-new document (`Ctrl+N`), quick-new collection (`Ctrl+M`), global search (`Ctrl+Shift+T`), flow mode (`Ctrl+I`), fullscreen writing (`F11`), source mode toggle (`Ctrl+/`). Click an input and press the new combination; conflicts are flagged, and a one-click reset restores defaults.

aiWorkbench.title: AI Workbench
aiWorkbench.body:
The AI workbench is the AI panel to the right of the writing area: chat with it like an assistant, or hand it a "smart task" that completes a whole operation for you. Set up [AI Model Setup](#/quickstart/aiSetup) first if you haven't.

## Chat

Just ask. The AI reads the context of the current work, so questions like "what is the main plotline of this volume" work too.

## Smart tasks

Give it a goal — say "compile this chapter's character list" — and the task runs on its own: searching the whole creation area, working step by step, and presenting the results. A timeline shows each state: queued, running, waiting for your input, verifying, ready to apply. Interrupted tasks resume where they stopped.

## Writes need your confirmation

Any change destined for the body text first opens a change review, where you allow it once, allow the same kind of change for this session, or reject it. Nothing is written until you approve, and every approved write returns a commit receipt. Token usage and tool-call counts are tracked per call in "Settings → AI call logs".

## Web access

With "Settings → Web tools" enabled, the AI can also:

- **Search**: the built-in engine by default (no setup); Bocha, Serper, Jina Reader or a custom HTTP endpoint can be connected instead;
- **Read pages**: fetch page content as HTML / plain text / JSON / PDF.

With web tools off, the AI works only with what's in the creation area.

aiSelection.title: Selection AI
aiSelection.body:
Select text and let the AI work on just that part.

| Mode | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| Continue | keeps writing from there |
| Polish | refines the language |
| Rewrite | says it a different way |
| Expand | fleshes out a passage |
| Condense | shortens it |
| De-AI | makes machine tone sound natural |
| Translate | Chinese ↔ English |

## Desktop

Select the text and pick a mode from the popup menu. Results appear in a compare view first — the body changes only after you accept; regenerate or discard otherwise. Each mode can bind a template from the [Prompt Library](#/ai/prompts) so the AI writes in your voice.

## Mobile

Select text to bring up the toolbar: AI rewrite, polish, expand, condense, continue, or ask the AI.

With nothing selected, tap "AI" in the bottom toolbar to work on the whole piece:

- **Summary**: generate a summary of the whole piece;
- **Proofread**: catch typos and grammar issues;
- **Expand & polish**: four tones (general / professional / concise / friendly);
- **Compose**: describe what you need and get new content.

Results stream in and can be stopped or regenerated; accept to insert into the body or replace the selection.

imageGen.title: AI Image Generation

translate.title: AI Translation
translate.body:
Translation runs on the AI models you configure, covering everything from a selected paragraph to a full PDF page.

## Selection translation

Select text in the body and choose "Translate" from the selection menu; the result shows in a compare view — accept to replace or insert. Selection AI runs on the global agent; models come from [AI Model Setup](#/quickstart/aiSetup).

## PDF translation

The PDF reader translates single pages or the whole document, with side-by-side Chinese / English reading; scanned pages are recognized by the vision model first, then translated, with the translation laid out in reading order — see [PDF Reading & Annotation](#/materials/pdf). Translation requests go straight to your configured provider; the platform never relays them.

mindmap.title: Mind Maps

canvas.title: Structured Canvas

pdf.title: PDF Reading & Annotation
pdf.body:
The PDF reader bundles annotation, page arrangement, AI region recognition (OCR), translation and AI Q&A — all on the desktop.

## The document library

Drop PDFs into the "资料库" (materials) folder in your creation area and they become the local document library; files stay exactly as they are on your own disk.

## Reading and annotation

- TOC navigation and full-text search;
- Select text to highlight and annotate; annotations collect in the sidebar;
- Box-select a region to annotate charts and figures screenshot-style.

## Page arrangement

Drag to reorder pages in the grid view; batch rotate, delete, insert and merge documents; add page numbers and watermarks; redact sensitive content.

## AI reading companion

- Whole-page AI summaries;
- Reading Q&A: ask about the full document — answers cite page numbers you can click through to verify.

For text recognition see [OCR](#/materials/ocr); for translation see [AI Translation](#/ai/translate).

ocr.title: OCR
ocr.body:
OCR turns text in images and scanned PDFs into editable text. On the desktop, recognition is handled by your vision model — no local model download; offline capability depends on whether your configured model runs locally.

## Before you start

Recognition is done by an AI vision model, so configure one that accepts image input first — see [AI Model Setup](#/quickstart/aiSetup). Recognition requests go straight to your provider.

## In PDFs

Open a scanned PDF (when the text layer is thin, the app suggests AI region recognition), box-select the area to read, and the result shows alongside the original — copyable and annotatable. PDF translation calls the vision model the same way for scanned pages: recognize first, then translate.

## In images

Images in the library and clippings work the same: recognize the whole image, or drag a box around part of it — the text lands directly in the body or your materials.

Keep scans sharp and upright; for complex layouts, box regions separately. Once recognized, the text is searchable via [Global Search](#/writing/search).

browser.title: Built-in Browser & Web Clipping
browser.body:
The built-in browser keeps your research in the app: search, browse, clip and save images, all from the "Web" page in the left navigation on the desktop.

## Browsing

Address bar, tabs, back / forward / refresh; the start page takes custom categories, favorite sites and a search engine order of your choosing. Pair it with [Multi-window & Split View](#/writing/multiwindow) — writing on the left, research on the right.

## Web clipping

Found a good article? One click captures the body text into the creation area as Markdown, with images saved locally. Clipping is enabled or disabled per site, managed in the extension settings.

## Saving images

Right-click any image on a page to save it into the image library.

images.title: Image Library

typeset.title: Article Typesetting Workbench
typeset.body:
The typesetting workbench turns a collection or a single chapter into print-ready, distributable output: paper, margins, headers and footers, page numbers and chapter order are configured on one page with a live preview. The capability is provided by the official Typeset Export plugin — install and enable it in the plugin center first (requires BigLazyCat Writer 0.4.5 or newer). For plugin development see [Plugin Development Process](#/plugins/dev).

## Entry points

- **Article**: choose 「排版导出」 (Typeset Export) in the article editor. The plugin captures a Markdown snapshot including unsaved changes, then opens the page; every open captures fresh, so to export later edits, reopen it from the article;
- **Book from a folder**: right-click a folder (or the workspace root) in the creation area and choose 「排版导出」 to typeset that directory directly; opening from a file uses its containing folder. The command palette and plugin center work too — browse the directory in the page, then pick it.

## Built-in components

The typesetting engine (Typst), PDF rendering (PDFium) and body fonts (Noto Serif SC regular/bold, Noto Emoji, Noto Sans Mono, LXGW WenKai) all ship with the plugin — nothing to download.

## The six tabs

- **Book info**: title, author and other details referenced by header placeholders and the title page;
- **Content**: which chapters to include; a single-chapter export contains only that chapter's body — no TOC, volume titles or intro pages;
- **Layout**: paper (A4 / A5 / B5 / 16K) and margin presets, body font and styles, page numbers (footer visibility and format), e-book theme;
- **Headers & footers**: enable them, place content left / center / right, use the `{title}` `{author}` `{chapter}` `{page}` `{pages}` placeholders, add separators and a running head;
- **Order**: chapters export in list order — move them up and down, or restore the default order in one click;
- **Export**: articles export to PDF, Word, HTML, PNG (plus EPUB); folders export books as EPUB, PDF, Word, HTML.

## Preview and export

The preview on the right supports paging, zoom and fit-to-width — every change is visible immediately. Export opens the system save dialog, shows live progress and can be cancelled. Large files stream to a temporary file and replace the target only after the write completes; settings and covers persist in the plugin's workspace storage, independent of the page address.

| Format | Best for |
| --- | --- |
| PDF | printing and sharing — fixed layout, embedded fonts |
| Word | handing off for further editing (fonts depend on the reading app) |
| EPUB | e-book readers, reflowable |
| HTML | single file with inlined styles and images, readable offline |
| PNG | long-image sharing for a single article |

Covers accept JPG / PNG / WebP up to 12 MB and appear on the first page of PDF, Word and EPUB. The image designer adds long images, poster ratios and multiple layouts and color themes. For no-fuss exports, the one-click [Book Making & Export](#/publish/book) from the creation area is faster.

wechat.title: WeChat Setup & Publishing

book.title: Book Making & Export
book.body:
A work becomes a book through the official "排版导出" (typeset & export) plugin: a single article exports to PDF / Word / HTML / PNG / EPUB, a whole folder to EPUB / PDF / Word / HTML.

Install and enable the plugin from the plugin center first — see [Official Plugins](#/plugins/official).

## Export a book

1. In the creation area, right-click the work folder (or the root) and choose "排版导出";
2. Pick the chapters and their order on the Content tab;
3. Set paper, fonts, page numbers and cover on the Layout and Header/Footer tabs;
4. Choose EPUB / PDF / Word / HTML on the Export tab and write the file where you want it.

Every option is explained in [Typesetting Workbench](#/publish/typeset).

## Export a single article

Open the article, then choose "排版导出" from the editor's plugin menu to export that one piece as PDF, Word, HTML, PNG or EPUB. A single article contains only its own body — no table of contents, volume titles or intro pages.

## Publish to the bookstore

To let readers read it online, publish the work from the portal's web workbench and tick "书城上架" (list in bookstore) when publishing.

sdk.title: Plugin SDK Overview
sdk.body:
The plugin SDK is the entire interface surface between a plugin and the host: the backend entry `blc-plugin-sdk`, the page entry `blc-plugin-sdk/browser`, and the manifest schema. It ships as a public npm package (`npm install blc-plugin-sdk`); the authoritative types are the bundled `index.d.ts` and `browser.d.ts`. The API major version is 1, extended by revisions: revision 1 added chunked document export, revision 2 color scheme, page readiness and user-entry declarations, revision 3 document navigation. This page covers the overview and core concepts; field-level details live in [SDK Manifest Schema](#/plugins/sdkManifest), [SDK Backend API](#/plugins/sdkBackend) and [SDK Page API](#/plugins/sdkPage).

## Two entries

| Entry | Runs in | Import | Capability boundary |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `blc-plugin-sdk` | plugin backend (Node 22, own process) | `import { definePlugin } from 'blc-plugin-sdk'` | Full Node file, network and subprocess capabilities |
| `blc-plugin-sdk/browser` | plugin page (browser renderer) | `import { connect } from 'blc-plugin-sdk/browser'` | Only this page's view session and the SDK APIs; Node modules must not be imported |

Pages may also import the host bridge from `./__sdk.mjs` next to the page (synchronous connect). Backend and page bridge to the host separately without shared memory; both share the "shared API" below. The SDK also ships helpers: `PluginError` (error with a machine-readable `code`), `waitForTask` (polls a task to completion, 30 s default timeout, 150 ms interval; cancel and timeout never replay the task) and `readDocument` (wraps chunked export with boundary checks, timeout and SHA-256 verification).

## Invocation & task states

Every command and service method receives an invocation:

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| signal | AbortSignal; long tasks should call `signal.throwIfAborted()` regularly for cooperative cancellation |
| invocationId | Unique id of this call |
| taskId | Host task id (command calls only) |
| progress(value, message?) | Report 0–1 progress and a message |
| source | Call origin |
| workspaceId / workspaceSession | Workspace identity; after a switch, old sessions are rejected (`WORKSPACE_CHANGED`) |
| windowId / editorId / documentId / revision / selection | Window, editor, document, revision and selection identity carried by menu triggers |
| sessionId / resource | Session and resource identity |

Tasks are host-owned: closing a page or AI conversation does not end the background task. States: `waiting`, `running`, `cancelling`, `completed`, `failed`, `cancelled`, `interrupted`, `uncertain`. Cancel, exit and timeout can leave `uncertain` external results (the other side may have executed); operations with side effects are never retried automatically. Commands have no single overall deadline — heartbeats only check event-loop responsiveness; a cancel timeout ends other tasks in the same instance.

## Core types

```ts
interface DocumentSnapshot extends DocumentTarget {
  content: string
  format: 'markdown' | 'tiptap'
  formatVersion?: 1
  revision: string
  draftHash: string
  dirty: boolean
}
interface DocumentExportChunk {
  exportId: string; format: 'markdown'; formatVersion: 1
  chunk: string; offset: number; nextOffset: number; totalBytes: number
  hash: string; revision: string; draftHash: string; dirty: boolean
}
interface DocumentChange extends DocumentTarget {
  operationId: string
  revision: string
  draftHash: string
  content: string
}
interface Operation {
  operationId: string
  state: 'pending' | 'completed' | 'failed' | 'uncertain'
  result?: Json
  error?: string
}
interface Task {
  id: string; pluginId: string; version: string; generation: string; command: string
  context: InvocationContext
  state: 'waiting' | 'running' | 'cancelling' | 'completed' | 'failed'
    | 'cancelled' | 'interrupted' | 'uncertain'
  progress: number; hasResult: boolean; result?: Json; error?: string; errorCode?: string
}
interface ViewOptions {
  location?: 'tab' | 'panel' | 'window'
  context?: InvocationContext
  state?: Json
  instanceId?: string
}
interface ViewSession {
  pluginId: string; viewId: string; instanceId: string; title: string; location: string
  context: InvocationContext
  state?: Json; dirty: boolean; connected: boolean
  theme?: Record<string, string>
  colorScheme: 'light' | 'dark'
  uiReady: boolean
  timings?: Record<string, number>
}
```

`DocumentTarget` is `{ workspaceId, workspaceSession, documentId, editorId, windowId? }`; `DocumentNavigationTarget` (revision 3) is `{ workspaceId, workspaceSession, documentId }`; `ResourceRequest` is `{ workspaceId, workspaceSession, path?, query?, offset?, limit?, content?, expectedHash?, operationId? }`; `Json` is null, boolean, number, string, arrays or plain objects, recursively.

## Error codes

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| API_MISMATCH | Manifest apiVersion differs from the host |
| NODE_MISMATCH | Node/npm versions do not satisfy the requirement |
| BACKPRESSURE | Concurrency limit exceeded |
| STALE_GENERATION | Response from a stale generation |
| WORKSPACE_CHANGED | The workspace has switched |
| DRAFT_CONFLICT | Document snapshot stale or draft conflict |
| RESOURCE_CHANGED | Resource changed while being read |
| MESSAGE_TOO_LARGE | Response exceeds the control-frame limit |
| DIRTY_VIEW | Page has unsaved changes (e.g. refusing close) |
| SAVE_TIMEOUT | Save confirmation timed out |
| OPERATION_CONFLICT | Operation conflict (e.g. same operationId, different arguments) |
| NAVIGATION_CANCELLED / NAVIGATION_TIMEOUT | Document navigation cancelled / timed out |

`PluginError.code` is machine-readable; throw stable string codes of your own so external AI and diagnostics can locate failures.

## Limits & quotas

| Item | Cap |
| --- | --- |
| Plugin background processes | 16 |
| Plugin pages | 32 |
| Unfinished command tasks | 128 |
| Install / development prep tasks | 8, scripts serialized and cancellable |
| Page restore state | 64 KiB |
| Control frames | 1 MiB |
| Single command result | under 1 MiB |
| Document export snapshots | 4 per plugin, 64 MiB per host, 2-minute expiry |
| Document export chunks | 96 KiB per chunk, 32 MiB total |
| Resource writes | 700 KiB per call |
| Text reads | 512 KiB per call, 16 MiB total |
| Image reads | 384 KiB per chunk, 28 MiB total, 100 per page |
| Service calls | 20 seconds, depth 8 |
| Plugin logs | 500 entries / 256 KiB per plugin |
| V8 heap | 256 MiB default |
| Process-tree memory / total CPU | 512 MiB / 25% |

Windows enforces quotas with a Job Object; macOS/Linux sample once per second and only stop after CPU exceeds the threshold 10 consecutive times — the sampling threshold is not a hard memory cap on every platform. A crashed background restarts with 2 s / 4 s backoff at most twice, re-activating only — commands, events and external operations are not replayed; the consecutive-failure counter survives app restarts and needs an explicit enable or restart to reset. Build pages for ES2022, Chromium 109 / Safari 16.4 or equivalent WebKit; final platform support follows the host's native UI acceptance.

## Where to look next

- Manifest fields and contribution points: [SDK Manifest Schema](#/plugins/sdkManifest);
- Backend context, documents and resources, services and schedules: [SDK Backend API](#/plugins/sdkBackend);
- Page bridge, restore state, save contract and document navigation: [SDK Page API](#/plugins/sdkPage).

sdkManifest.title: SDK Manifest Schema
sdkManifest.body:
Field-level reference for the `biglazycat` manifest; for the project-setup workflow see [Plugin Development Process](#/plugins/dev).

## Manifest fields (biglazycat in package.json)

The manifest is the `biglazycat` object in `package.json`; unknown fields are rejected. Top-level fields:

| Field | Type | Required | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| apiVersion | 1 | yes | SDK major version, currently fixed at 1; mismatch reports `API_MISMATCH` |
| minimumApiRevision | integer | no | Minimum API revision required; the host refuses to install when lower |
| displayName | string | yes | Display name, 1–200 characters |
| description | string | no | Plugin description |
| main | string | no | Backend entry relative path; must not start with `/`, contain `..`, `\` or `:`; page-only plugins may omit it |
| mainView | string | no | Main view id, matching `^[a-zA-Z0-9][a-zA-Z0-9._-]{0,99}$` |
| settingsView | string | no | Settings view id |
| platforms | string[] | yes | Targets from `windows/amd64`, `windows/arm64`, `darwin/amd64`, `darwin/arm64`, `linux/amd64`, `linux/arm64`, 1–256 items |
| activation | string[] | no | Auto-activation events: `startup`, `workspace.opened`, `document.committed` |
| dependencies | object[] | no | Runtime plugin-service dependencies, each with plugin, service, version, optional; 0–256 items |
| contributes | object | yes | Contribution points, see below |

Beyond the schema the host also validates platforms, engines, path existence, references and duplicate ids.

### contributes

| Key | Fields (bold = required) | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| commands | **id**, **title**, description, contexts, aiCallable, externalEffect, visibility, inputSchema | Commands. contexts: workspace, editor.document, editor.selection, resource — where the command applies; aiCallable exposes it to external AI; externalEffect marks outside side effects; `visibility: "internal"` (revision 2) hides the command from the palette, shortcuts and toolbar while pages can still call it — independent of aiCallable; inputSchema is a restricted JSON Schema supporting type, description, properties, required, additionalProperties, items, enum, minimum, maximum, minLength, maxLength, minItems, maxItems |
| views | **id**, **title**, **entry**, **defaultLocation**, route, multiple, commandPalette | Pages. entry points to an HTML file in the build output; defaultLocation: tab, panel, window; multiple allows several instances; `commandPalette: false` (revision 2) avoids duplicating the page with its open command; route starts with `/` |
| menus | **location**, **command** | Menu entries. location: editor.selection, editor.document, resource, toolbar; command references a declared command id |
| services | **id**, **version**, **methods** | Services offered to other plugins; methods holds 1–256 method names |
| providers | **id**, **contract**, **version**, **service** | Export providers; contract is currently `export.text`, version fixed at 1, service references a declared service |
| editors | **id**, **title**, **extensions**, **view** | Custom file editors; extensions like `.catnote`, 1–256 items; view references a declared page |
| schedules | **id**, **command**, **intervalSeconds**, **catchUp** | Scheduled tasks; intervalSeconds 10–31536000; catchUp: skip, once |

### Service dependencies

`dependencies` is unrelated to npm `dependencies`; it declares other plugins' services you call at runtime:

```json
"dependencies": [
  { "plugin": "@scope/text-tools", "service": "text", "version": "^1.0.0", "optional": true }
]
```

Missing required dependencies, version mismatches or dependency cycles are rejected at enable/startup; optional dependencies never auto-start incompatible versions — callers handle unavailability.

sdkBackend.title: SDK Backend API
sdkBackend.body:
API reference for the plugin backend (a Node process): the context object, document and resource access, services and scheduled tasks. For concepts and the task model see [Plugin SDK Overview](#/plugins/sdk).

## The PluginContext

`definePlugin(activate)` receives a context and may return a cleanup function (sync or async) that runs on deactivation:

```ts
export default definePlugin((context: PluginContext) => {
  // register every command and service declared in the manifest
  return async () => {
    // release connections, listeners, etc.
  }
})
```

| Property | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| apiVersion | 1 | API major version |
| apiRevision | number | API revision supported by the host |
| pluginId | string | Plugin identity assigned at install |
| generation | string | Activation generation; changes after fault restarts and invalidates stale responses (`STALE_GENERATION`) |
| dataDir | string | Private data directory; the host backs it up before updates |

### commands

| Method | Signature | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| register | register(id, handler) | Register a command; handler receives (args, invocation). Register everything during activation, matching contributes.commands |

A command's return value becomes the host-held task result, under 1 MiB per call; large documents and images are chunked by the plugin. Task lifecycle is described under "Invocation & task states".

### services

| Method | Signature | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| provide | provide(id, methods) | Provide a service; method keys match the manifest, values are (args, invocation) handlers |
| call | call(plugin, service, method, args, invocation?) | Call another plugin's service; passing invocation propagates the call chain |
| list | list() | List currently available services |

Service calls are limited to 20 seconds and depth 8; cycles fail immediately. The shared export contract `export.text` v1: the service method `transform({text, format: 'markdown', filename}, invocation)` returns `{text}`; it is used only after the user picks the provider in the plugin center, and provider failures surface as errors rather than silently falling back.

### events

| Method | Signature | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| on | on(name, handler) | Subscribe; handler receives (event, {signal}) with id, name, workspaceId, payload |
| emit | emit(name, payload) | Emit; the plugin namespace is added automatically as plugin:pkgname:name |

Built-in events: `startup`, `workspace.opened`, `document.committed`, plus other plugins' `plugin:pkgname:name`. Workspace restores also emit open events; `document.committed` only covers wired commit paths, not every Node file change. When the queue is full events are dropped and logged; delivery is not guaranteed — consumers re-read domain state and keep business checkpoints in storage.

### credentials

| Method | Signature | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| get | get(key) | Read a credential, string or null |
| set | set(key, value) | Write a credential |
| delete | delete(key) | Delete a credential |

Credentials live only in the backend process: Windows uses DPAPI bound to the current user, macOS the login Keychain, Linux the system secret service. Credentials must never enter the manifest, sources or page state.

### Shared API (same names and semantics in both contexts)

| Namespace | Methods | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| documents | snapshot(target) / export(request) / apply(change) / operation(operationId) | Core document reads and writes; export reads an immutable Markdown snapshot in chunks — see "Document operations" |
| workspace | list() / resources(req) / read(req) / search(req) / import(req) | Workspace and resource files — see "Resources & images" |
| images | list(req) / read(req) | Paged image library and chunked reads — see "Resources & images" |
| storage | get(key, workspaceId?) / set(key, value, workspaceId?) | Plugin KV store with JSON values; with and without workspaceId are separate namespaces |
| views | open(view, options?) | Open a page, returns a ViewSession; the backend also has close(instanceId), which refuses dirty pages |
| ui | notify(message) / openFile(options?) / saveFile(options?) / openExternal(url) / openDocument(target) | System notification; open/save dialogs return the chosen path; openExternal accepts HTTP(S) only and opens the system browser; openDocument (revision 3) locates and opens a document in the main window |

Backend-only: `ai.run({conversationId, text})` sends a message into an existing AI conversation and returns a JSON result.

## Document operations (documents)

Core documents (chapter text and the like) follow optimistic concurrency in three steps: snapshot first, then apply with revision, draftHash and a unique operationId:

```ts
const snap = await ctx.documents.snapshot({
  workspaceId, workspaceSession, documentId, editorId, windowId,
})
const op = await ctx.documents.apply({
  workspaceId, workspaceSession, documentId, editorId, windowId,
  operationId: crypto.randomUUID(),
  revision: snap.revision,
  draftHash: snap.draftHash,
  content: nextText,
})
```

- The same operationId with the same normalized arguments returns the original record instead of resubmitting; different arguments are rejected (`OPERATION_CONFLICT`);
- Visible conflicts arise when the document, tags, workspace, draft or persisted version changed, or other dirty editors, external edits or tab switches happened;
- Changes go through the target editor's transaction and the existing save flow, preserving that editor's undo; arbitrary cross-file side effects are not guaranteed reversible;
- After an apply timeout, confirm via `documents.operation(operationId)` before retrying; unconfirmed operations after a crash become `uncertain`;
- Operation receipts are capped at 10000 in the current log directory; new operations are refused at the cap;
- Writing files directly with Node bypasses all of these guarantees.

For publishing, reading and exporting prefer chunked export (revision 1): `documents.export` creates an immutable Markdown v1 snapshot returned as UTF-8 byte-offset chunks (96 KiB each, 32 MiB total) with SHA-256; up to 4 unfinished snapshots per plugin and 64 MiB per host, the last chunk releases the snapshot, unfinished snapshots expire after two minutes. The `readDocument(documents, target, options)` helper wraps chunking and verification and returns the full `{content, hash, revision, draftHash, dirty}`:

```ts
import { readDocument } from 'blc-plugin-sdk'
const doc = await readDocument(ctx.documents, target, { timeoutMs: 30000, signal })
// doc.content is Markdown v1 — no need to understand host Tiptap nodes
```

Opening a page may unmount the source editor, so capture the document with `readDocument` first and open the page with `views.open` afterwards; never rely on the original `editorId` remaining available.

## Resources & images (workspace and images)

| Method | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| workspace.list() | List workspaces (WorkspaceRecord: id, rootPath, title, createdAt, lastOpenedAt) |
| workspace.read(req) | Read UTF-8 text, returns content and hash (for import's expectedHash); 512 KiB per call, 16 MiB total per text file |
| workspace.resources(req) | List resources by path; entries are ResourceEntry records with the published API 1 casing (Rel, Parent, Name, Title, Kind, Editable, Ext, IsDir, Size, ModTimeUnix, Hash, …) |
| workspace.search(req) | Search resources by keyword |
| workspace.import(req) | Write UTF-8 text: with expectedHash it is a conditional overwrite (mismatch fails); without it a new file is created and existing files cannot be overwritten; 700 KiB per call, operationId required |
| images.list(req) | Paged images, 100 per page, returns {items: {id, name, src, width, height}, total} |
| images.read(req) | Image as data URL in chunks (addressed by src), 384 KiB per chunk, 28 MiB total; pass the first chunk's hash onward, changes report `RESOURCE_CHANGED` |

`ResourceEntry.ModTimeUnix` is Unix nanoseconds: divide by `1_000_000` for JavaScript milliseconds and validate before `toISOString()`. Browser pages bind to their workspace identity automatically and may omit workspaceId/workspaceSession; the Node side must pass them explicitly. After a workspace switch, reads from the old page are rejected. Larger or binary resources go through Node file APIs with your own concurrency handling.

Typical custom-editor write:

```ts
const result = await sdk.workspace.import({
  workspaceId, workspaceSession, path: 'notes/example.catnote',
  expectedHash: loadedHash, content: nextText, operationId: crypto.randomUUID(),
})
```

## Scheduled tasks (schedules)

The manifest declares {id, command, intervalSeconds, catchUp}. Checkpoints live in the install index and survive restarts: past the interval plus a 5-second grace, `skip` drops the run and `once` catches up at most once; the same command never overlaps itself. The checkpoint is saved before scheduling — if saving fails nothing runs; a crash between the two steps may skip one round and exactly-once is not guaranteed. Long tasks keep business checkpoints in storage and re-read domain state on activation.

markdownBasics.title: Markdown Basics
markdownBasics.body:
Markdown marks up formatting with symbols: two asterisks for bold, a hash for a heading. You keep writing; the symbols carry the format, and the software handles the layout.

The app is WYSIWYG by default: symbols turn into formatted output as you type; source mode shows and edits the raw markup.

## Why Markdown

- Every format without leaving the keyboard — no train of thought broken;
- Plain text, opens in any editor;
- Small files, easy to back up and sync.

## Headings and paragraphs

A blank line starts a new paragraph. A hash plus a space at line start makes a heading; the number of hashes is the level (`#` through `######`, six levels) — levels two and three see most of the action.

## Emphasis

| Effect | Markup |
| --- | --- |
| **Bold** | `**text**` |
| *Italic* | `*text*` |
| ~~Strikethrough~~ | `~~text~~` |
| `Inline code` | wrap the text in backticks |

## Lists and quotes

- Unordered list: dash + space at line start; indent one level per nesting;
- Ordered list: number + dot + space;
- Task list: dash, space, brackets (an `x` inside marks it done);
- Quote: greater-than + space, for excerpts.

## Links and images

- Link: `[text](url)`, e.g. `[BigLazyCat](https://example.com)`;
- Image: a link with an exclamation mark in front — or just paste / drag an image file in.

## Rules and code blocks

Three dashes alone on a line make a horizontal rule. Three backticks alone on a line open a code block, and three close it; append a language name (`js`, `python`…) after the opening backticks for syntax highlighting.

Tables, formulas, task lists and more are covered in [Advanced Markdown](#/syntax/markdownAdvanced).

markdownAdvanced.title: Advanced Markdown
markdownAdvanced.body:
The advanced formats you'll use most in writing.

## Tables

Separate cells with pipes; the second row declares the header with dashes. Colons control alignment: `:-` left, `:-:` center, `-:` right.

## Code blocks and diagrams

A language name after the opening backticks enables highlighting; `mermaid` renders the whole block as a diagram — see [Mermaid Basics](#/syntax/mermaidBasics).

## Task lists

Dash, space, brackets at line start: empty is unfinished, `x` is done. Great for revision checklists and pre-publication passes.

## Math

- Inline: wrap in single `$`, e.g. `$E=mc^2$`;
- Block: wrap in `$$` on their own lines.

The formula editor in the toolbar inserts common symbols visually — no LaTeX memorization needed.

## Heading levels and the outline

Long works organize with level-2 and level-3 headings; the outline panel turns them into a jumpable TOC. Don't skip levels (a level-3 directly under a level-1 tangles the outline).

## Typography habits

- Put spaces between Chinese and Latin characters or numbers;
- Keep paragraphs to three to five lines; split long ones;
- Bold marks what matters — no more than three per page.

mermaidBasics.title: Mermaid Basics
mermaidBasics.body:
Mermaid draws diagrams from text: a few lines of code render into flowcharts, sequence diagrams and more. Insert a code block with the `mermaid` language in the editor.

## Three rules

1. The first line declares the diagram type — `graph TD` is a top-down flowchart;
2. Nodes are a letter plus brackets (`A[text]`); arrows `-->` connect them;
3. Lines starting with `%%` are comments and don't render.

The desktop renders automatically as you type the block; on mobile you edit the source and preview directly.

## Flowchart

```
graph TD
    A[Wake up] --> B{Good weather?}
    B -- Yes --> C[Go for a run]
    B -- No --> D[Keep writing]
```

Square brackets are ordinary nodes, curly braces are decisions, and the label between the dashes on an arrow describes the branch.

## Sequence diagram

```
sequenceDiagram
    Author->>Editor: writes an idea
    Editor-->>Author: autosaves
```

`->>` is a solid arrow, `-->>` a dashed one; the message follows the colon.

## State diagram

```
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Ideation
    Ideation --> Writing: new chapter
    Writing --> Revising: draft done
    Revising --> [*]
```

`[*]` marks start and end; the text after a colon on an arrow is the trigger.

More diagram types: [Mermaid Charts Cheat Sheet](#/syntax/mermaidCharts).

## When it doesn't render

Usually a typo: check the declaration line, make sure arrow symbols are complete, and look for stray special characters in node labels. Fix one thing at a time — faster than rewriting the block.

mermaidCharts.title: Mermaid Cheat Sheet
mermaidCharts.body:
Pick a diagram type by what you want to express: think about the relationship first, then choose.

## Cheat sheet

| To express | Diagram | Declaration |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Steps and branches | Flowchart | `graph TD` or `graph LR` |
| Messages between actors | Sequence | `sequenceDiagram` |
| State transitions | State | `stateDiagram-v2` |
| Classes and inheritance | Class | `classDiagram` |
| Data entity relations | ER | `erDiagram` |
| Schedules and milestones | Gantt | `gantt` |
| Composition shares | Pie | `pie` |

## Flowchart

```
graph LR
    Setup --> Conflict --> Twist --> Ending
```

Direction letters: `TD` top-down, `LR` left-to-right.

## Sequence diagram

```
sequenceDiagram
    Reader->>Author: follows updates
    Author-->>Reader: posts two chapters
```

## State and ER diagrams

```
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Serializing
    Serializing --> Completed: book finished
```

```
erDiagram
    Reader ||--o{ Review : writes
    Work ||--o{ Review : receives
```

## Gantt and pie

```
gantt
    Three-volume writing plan
    Volume 1 :done, vol1, 2026-01-01, 60d
    Volume 2 :active, vol2, after vol1, 60d
    Volume 3 :vol3, after vol2, 60d
```

```
pie
    Writing time split
    Drafting : 50
    Research : 30
    Revising : 20
```

When a render fails, check the declaration line first; diagram data lives in the Markdown source, so edits re-render any time.
